study.title: Isaiah 46 - The God Who carries his people and defeats idols
study.overview: Isaiah 46 incisively opposes the gods of Babylon and the Lord of Israel. The idols Bel and Nebo, who should protect their worshippers, appear as heavy burdens that need to be carried by animals and people; on the contrary, the Lord declares that he himself carried Israel from the beginning of its history and would continue to support his people to old age. The chapter then exposes the uselessness of idolatry, calls the people to remember who God is and announces that the Lord will fulfill his purpose, calling from afar the instrument of his will. The outcome promises that God's righteousness and salvation will not be distant, but will come to Zion as glory for Israel.

outline.title: The idols are heavy; the Lord is the one who carries
outline.explanation: Bel and Nebo cannot sustain anyone; they themselves go into captivity. In contrast, the Lord calls Israel to hear him: he has carried the people from the womb, will continue to sustain them in old age and promise constant deliverance.

outline.title: The falsehood of idolatry
outline.explanation: The Lord challenges any comparison with any image or god made. Idols are made with gold and silver, carried by men, placed standing, but immovable and dumb; they answer neither deliver nor deliver in affliction.

outline.title: Remember who God is and trust in your salvation
outline.explanation: The people are called to bring to memory the past and to act firmly, because the Lord knows the end from the beginning and executes its purpose. He calls from the east the man who fulfills his intention, and therefore his righteousness and salvation will come near, bringing glory to Israel.

study.context: The notes place the chapter on the horizon of Babylonian exile and the promise of liberation. The rest of Israel is described as the group that would survive after the destruction of Jerusalem, and many exiles were discouraged in the face of the promise of ransom. The references to Bel and Nebo point to the Babylonian religion, used by the prophet as a contrast to the living God who holds his people. The notes also identify the "man of my intention" as Cyrus, the Persian king, linked to the liberation of the Jews from captivity.
study.theology: The chapter teaches God's absolute sovereignty over history and its radical difference in relation to idols. The false gods are unable to act, speak or save; but the Lord knows in advance the events, directs the peoples and fulfills what he determines. There is also a strong theme of covenant grace: God not only created Israel, but sustained it continually, promising to preserve it until the end. The "justice" of God here is not a mere abstract concept; in the notes, it appears as the saving intervention by which God puts everything in order and brings concrete salvation to Zion. The glory of Israel therefore does not come from man-made religious ornaments, but from God himself who commits himself to his people.

scholarViews.insight: The rest of Israel in 46:3 points to the remnant that would survive after the destruction of Jerusalem, and the main contrast is between idols that need to be carried and the Lord carrying his people.
In 46:5-7, idolatry is exposed as absurd: the infinite God cannot be reduced to an image made by human hands, for the idol is manufactured, placed and worshipped, but cannot answer or deliver.
In 46:8, the call to remember and act firmly confronts the discouraged people; the exhortation seeks to lead them to reflect and abandon unbelief before the promise of God.

questions: If God has carried Israel from the womb, in which areas of my life I am still trying to carry alone what should I give to him?
What modern forms of idolatry seem to promise help, but in practice they are unable to respond at the time of distress?
How is the certainty that God knows the end from the beginning strengthens my confidence when the situation seems out of control?
study.practice: This week, take a moment to name, in prayer, what has occupied the place of trust in your heart. Then he rereads the whole chapter and transforms the accusation against idols into personal confession: God is the one who sustains, directs and saves. Also choose a concrete promise from the text - especially that the salvation of God will not delay and repeat it in prayer when discouragement comes, asking God to produce in you an obedient and firm faith.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not detail the meaning of all poetic terms and do not allow for certain definition of all historical aspects beyond Babylonian exile and the reference to Cyrus. Some observations of commentators about the Hebrew text appear in divergent translations, but here they were used only as interpretive support, without stating more than the notes allow.
